After taking part in the general lament over the dreadful consequences of this affair, which Elizabeth judged almost inevitable, and Miss Bennet could not declare entirely impossible, the former pursued the subject. ‘But tell me everything about it that I have not heard already. Let me have more particulars. What did Colonel Forster say? Had they suspected nothing before the elopement? They must constantly have seen the two together.’

‘Colonel Forster admitted that he had frequently suspected an attachment, particularly on Lydia’s part, but nothing that alarmed him. I feel so sorry for him. He was as attentive and kind as anyone could be. He was already coming here to express his concern, before he had any notion that they had not gone to Scotland; when that suspicion began to circulate, it quickened his journey.’

‘And was Denny certain that Wickham would not marry her? Did he know they meant to run away? Had Colonel Forster spoken to Denny himself?’

‘Yes; but when the Colonel questioned him, Denny denied any knowledge of their scheme, and refused to give his true opinion of it. He did not again declare his conviction that they would not marry, and this encourages me to hope that he was misunderstood the first time.’

‘And until Colonel Forster arrived in person, I suppose none of you doubted that they were actually married?’

‘How could such a thought have occurred to us? I was a little troubled—a little afraid for my sister’s happiness as his wife, because I knew his behaviour had not invariably been right. My father and mother knew nothing of that; they thought only of the imprudence of the match. Kitty then confessed, with a very natural satisfaction at knowing more than everyone else, that Lydia’s last letter had prepared her for a step of this kind. Apparently she had known for many weeks that they were in love.’

‘But not before their journey to Brighton?’

‘No, I do not think so.’

‘And did Colonel Forster himself seem to have a poor opinion of Wickham? Is he acquainted with his true character?’

‘I must acknowledge that he spoke less favourably of Wickham than he used to. He considered him extravagant and imprudent; and since this unhappy business, there has been talk that he left Meryton heavily in debt. But I hope that is untrue.’

‘Oh, Jane, if we had kept less to ourselves, if we had told what we knew about him, this could never have occurred!’

‘Perhaps that would have been wiser,’ answered her sister.

‘But it seemed unjustifiable to reveal anyone’s past faults without knowing what their feelings might now be.’

If you do not, and you ask for my restraint and the mercy of those you have so deeply harmed, sit down in that chair without another word. It has been waiting for you for two full days.’

Monks muttered something unintelligible, but remained undecided.

‘Make your choice quickly,’ said Mr. Brownlow. ‘One word from me, and you lose this alternative forever.’

The man still hesitated.

‘I have no desire to negotiate,’ said Mr. Brownlow, ‘and since I am defending the most precious interests of other people, I have no right to.’

‘Is there—’ Monks asked, stumbling over the words, ‘is there—no compromise?’

‘None.’

Monks studied the old gentleman anxiously. Finding only severity and determination in his face, he came into the room, shrugged his shoulders, and sat down.

‘Lock the door from outside,’ Mr. Brownlow told the attendants, ‘and return when I ring.’

The men did as he said, leaving the two alone together.

‘A fine way to treat me, sir,’ said Monks, throwing down his hat and cloak, ‘for my father’s oldest friend.’

‘It is because I was your father’s oldest friend, young man,’ Mr. Brownlow replied; ‘because the hopes and wishes of my youth and happiness were bound up with him, and with that lovely woman of his family who returned to God so young, leaving me here alone and lonely; because, while still a boy, he knelt beside me at his only sister’s deathbed on the morning when—but Heaven chose otherwise—she would have become my young wife; because from then until his death my wounded heart remained attached to him through all his troubles and mistakes; because my heart was filled with old memories and connections, and even seeing you brings back thoughts of him. It is for all these reasons that I feel compelled to treat you gently now—yes, Edward Leeford, even now—and to feel ashamed that you are unworthy of the name you bear.’

‘What does the name have to do with anything?’ the other asked, after watching his companion’s distress with a mixture of silence and stubborn bewilderment. ‘What does the name mean to me?’

‘Nothing,’ Mr. Brownlow answered. ‘Nothing to you. But it was hers, and even after all these years it brings back to me, an old man, the warmth and excitement I once felt merely hearing a stranger speak it. I am very glad you have changed it—very, very glad.’

‘This is all very fine,’ said Monks, to keep using his adopted name, after a long silence. Throughout it he had been jerking back and forth in sullen defiance, while Mr. Brownlow sat with his hand covering his face.

‘What is it?’

‘Ten o’clock, sir.’

‘What are you saying? Ten o’clock at night?’

‘Yes, sir. Your honour asked me to wake you.’

‘Oh! Now I remember. Very good, very good.’

He made several sluggish attempts to fall asleep again, which the man skilfully defeated by tending the fire without pause for five minutes. Then he rose, flung on his hat, and went out. He entered the Temple and, having refreshed himself by walking twice along the pavements of King’s Bench-walk and Paper-buildings, made his way into Stryver’s chambers.

Stryver’s clerk, who never took part in these consultations, had gone home, and Stryver himself answered the door. He wore slippers and a loose dressing-gown, with his throat uncovered for comfort. Around his eyes were those somewhat wild, strained, scorched lines to be seen in all hard-living men of his profession, from the portrait of Jeffries onwards, and traceable, beneath Art’s various disguises, in the portraits of every Drinking Age.

‘You are rather late, Memory,’ Stryver remarked.

‘Much the ordinary time; perhaps a quarter of an hour behind.’

They entered a dingy room lined with volumes and strewn with papers, where a bright fire burned. A kettle steamed on the hob, and amid the wreckage of documents stood a gleaming table well supplied with wine, brandy, rum, sugar, and lemons.

‘I can see you have had your bottle, Sydney.’

‘Two this evening, I believe. I have been dining with today’s client; or watching him dine—it amounts to the same thing!’

‘That was a capital point you made about the identification, Sydney. How did you discover it? When did it occur to you?’

‘I thought him a fairly handsome fellow, and it occurred to me that I might have been much the same sort of fellow if fortune had favoured me.’

Mr. Stryver laughed until his prematurely grown paunch shook.

‘You and your fortune, Sydney! Set to work, set to work.’

With sufficient sullenness, the jackal loosened his clothes, passed into the next room, and returned carrying a large jug of cold water, a basin, and one or two towels. He soaked the towels, wrung them out incompletely, and arranged them over his head in a hideous fashion. Sitting at the table, he announced, ‘Now I am prepared!’

‘There is little boiling down for tonight, Memory,’ said Mr. Stryver cheerfully, searching through his papers.

‘How much?’

‘Just two sets.’

‘Let me have the worst one first.’

‘Here they are, Sydney. Go at them!’

The lion then settled upon his back on a sofa at one side of the drinking-table. Across it, the jackal sat at his own proper table, covered in papers, with glasses and bottles conveniently within reach.
